Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN)  -- Babies lie side by side in warming beds or sprawled on blankets atop crude wooden tables. Many families at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in Kabul, Afghanistan, seem resigned to the situation. Children with wounds and broken bones are carried in by their parents to wait on stiff plastic chairs. Outside, coughing youngsters squat on the pavement with their anxious families, waiting for care. And everywhere, parents clutch plastic bags containing bring-your-own medicines and supplies. For though they are all awaiting treatment at Afghanistan's only specialist pediatric hospital, the hospital cannot even afford bandages for its patients. The Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in central Kabul has to run on an operating budget of less than $1,200 a month, said Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, the hospital director. The few supplies that he can buy have to be hoarded for emergencies, and he has to count on parents to buy what's needed to care for their children. "In some cases, there is shortage of the surgical materials, and sometimes we don't have antiseptic to use," Yousufzai said. The United Nations says that more than $15 billion in aid has been sent to Afghanistan since the U.S.-led coalition overthrew the Taliban in late 2001. But still, the hospital cannot afford to help the hundreds of children who stream in every day, desperate for care and cures. The government does pay for salaries and sometimes for fuel, but there is often a shortage of even basic supplies like syringes. Doctors say they have to double up premature babies in incubators. And some of those incubators are compromised. On a recent day, a plastic surgical mask taped onto one machine was the only shield from infection.  Watch scenes from inside the hospital » . The parents waiting anxiously beside their sick children seem resigned to the situation in the hospital. One mother, who declined to give her name, said she spent the family's entire weekly income of $8 on an injection that did not help her baby. "This is something that the hospital should be giving us, because we can't afford it," she said. The U.S. Agency for International Development says infant mortality has dropped by 22 percent since the overthrow of the Taliban but acknowledges that the health status for Afghans is among the worst in the world. One in every five Afghan children will die before their 5th birthday, often of a preventable disease, according to the Save the Children aid agency. The toll on the children and parents is clear to any visitor, and the strain hits the hospital staff, too. "When you see a patient is very, very, sick and you cannot help, and they have to provide something for their children and they are not able to provide, it's also a stress for us," Yousufzai said. At the end of 2001, there were hopes that the hospital would be upgraded, but it is still waiting. It needs some acute care of its own, or it will continue to struggle to help the children who arrive at its door pleading for care.

**KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) —** At Kabul’s Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, infants share warming cots or rest on blankets spread across roughly built wooden tables. Families appear to have accepted the grim conditions. Parents carry in children suffering from fractures and open injuries, then sit with them on hard plastic seats. Beyond the hospital walls, coughing children crouch on the sidewalk alongside worried relatives as they wait to be seen.

Throughout the facility, mothers and fathers hold plastic bags filled with medicines and medical items they have purchased themselves. Although this is Afghanistan’s sole hospital specializing in pediatric care, it lacks the money to provide even basic dressings.

Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, the hospital’s director, said the central Kabul institution operates on less than $1,200 per month. Because its limited stock must be saved for critical cases, the hospital depends on families to obtain many of the materials required for their children’s treatment.

“At times, surgical supplies are unavailable, and on some occasions we do not even have antiseptic,” Yousufzai said.

According to the United Nations, Afghanistan has received more than $15 billion in assistance since the U.S.-led coalition removed the Taliban from power in late 2001. Yet the hospital remains unable to meet the needs of the hundreds of children who arrive each day seeking urgent treatment.

The Afghan government covers staff wages and occasionally provides fuel, but shortages frequently extend to fundamental items such as syringes. Physicians say premature infants sometimes have to share incubators, several of which are themselves unsafe or inadequate. During one recent visit, a disposable surgical mask taped over an incubator served as its only barrier against infection. **Watch footage from inside the hospital »**

Parents gathered beside their ill children seem to regard these circumstances as unavoidable. One woman, who did not want to be identified, said she used her family’s full weekly earnings—$8—to purchase an injection that failed to improve her baby’s condition.

“The hospital ought to supply this because it is beyond what we can pay for,” she said.

The U.S. Agency for International Development reports that infant deaths have declined by 22 percent since the Taliban’s fall. Nevertheless, the agency concedes that Afghanistan’s overall health conditions remain among the poorest worldwide.

Save the Children says one out of every five Afghan children dies before reaching age 5, frequently from illnesses that could have been prevented.

The emotional burden on both families and young patients is immediately visible, and hospital employees experience the pressure as well.

“It is stressful for us when someone is extremely ill and we cannot assist them, especially when the family must obtain something for the child but has no means to do so,” Yousufzai said.

There was optimism at the close of 2001 that the facility would be modernized, but those improvements have yet to materialize. The hospital itself urgently requires help; without it, staff will remain unable to adequately care for the children who come seeking treatment.

### Afghanistan’s Only Specialist Pediatric Hospital Struggles to Meet Demand

Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital in Kabul, Afghanistan’s only specialist pediatric hospital, treats hundreds of young patients every day. Despite its vital national role, the hospital is severely overcrowded and lacks the facilities, equipment, and resources required to provide adequate care.

The hospital operates on a budget of less than $1,200 per month. This amount is often insufficient to cover even basic medical supplies, including bandages, syringes, antiseptics, and essential surgical materials. As a result, parents are frequently asked to purchase medicines and other supplies themselves. For families already living in poverty, these costs can be overwhelming and may prevent children from receiving timely treatment.

Doctors and nurses are forced to ration the limited equipment available. In some cases, two premature babies must share a single incubator. Medical staff may also have to rely on damaged or inadequate machines that offer poor protection against infection, increasing the risks faced by already vulnerable patients.

The hospital’s situation is particularly striking given that more than $15 billion in international aid has entered Afghanistan since 2001. Nevertheless, Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital remains critically underfunded. Its experience highlights the gap between large-scale aid commitments and the resources reaching essential public health institutions, leaving medical workers unable to meet the urgent needs of Afghanistan’s children.
outputs.L4:
Afghanistan’s only specialist pediatric hospital is struggling to provide even the most basic treatment for sick children. Visits to the hospital and interviews with doctors, nurses, patients, and their families reveal wards filled beyond capacity, essential equipment that is broken or unavailable, and staff attempting to work with critically limited supplies.

Children with serious illnesses often share beds or are treated in crowded rooms and corridors. Medical workers must make difficult decisions about how to use the few functioning machines and the small quantities of medicine available. Equipment that would normally be considered essential in a pediatric hospital cannot always be repaired or replaced, leaving doctors and nurses to rely on improvised solutions.

Families also bear much of the financial burden. Parents are frequently asked to purchase medicines, syringes, laboratory materials, and other supplies outside the hospital before treatment can continue. For many Afghans, even these basic items are unaffordable. Some families have traveled long distances and spent most of their savings simply to reach the hospital. Once there, they may have to borrow money, sell possessions, or delay care while trying to obtain what doctors need.

Hospital staff say the institution receives less than $1,200 a month to cover its operating needs. That amount is insufficient for a facility responsible for treating some of the country’s most vulnerable patients. It must stretch limited funds across medicines, maintenance, equipment, sanitation, electricity, and other daily expenses. Employees continue working under intense pressure, but dedication alone cannot compensate for the absence of reliable funding and supplies.

The conditions are especially striking given the billions of dollars in international assistance directed toward Afghanistan over the years. Although aid has supported numerous health programs and development projects, the situation inside the pediatric hospital shows how little of that investment has translated into dependable care at the bedside. Complex funding systems, shifting priorities, weak institutions, corruption, and poor oversight have all contributed to a gap between the sums announced and the services actually available to ordinary Afghans.

For children and their families, that gap has immediate consequences. A broken machine can mean that a diagnosis is delayed. A missing medicine can allow a treatable condition to become life-threatening. A request to buy supplies can force parents to choose between medical care and food for the rest of the family.

The hospital’s struggle is therefore more than the story of one underfunded institution. It reflects the broader failure of Afghanistan’s health system and of international assistance to establish sustainable, accessible services. Despite enormous spending and years of promises, the country’s sickest children are still being treated in overcrowded wards without reliable access to essential medicines, functioning equipment, or adequate financial support.

Doctors and families continue to hope for urgent help, but they also stress that temporary donations are not enough. The hospital needs stable funding, properly maintained equipment, consistent supplies, and a system that does not require impoverished parents to finance treatment themselves. Until those needs are met, Afghanistan’s only specialist pediatric hospital will remain a stark symbol of how international aid has failed to secure even the most basic care for the children who need it most.

counterfactuals.output:
# Kabul children’s hospital overwhelmed despite decades of aid to Afghanistan

**KABUL, Afghanistan —** At Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, Afghanistan’s largest pediatric referral centre, families crowd into corridors while doctors move between wards filled with malnourished children, newborns with infections and patients suffering from preventable illnesses.

The hospital treats hundreds of children on busy days, many referred from provinces where health facilities lack specialists, medicine or reliable electricity. Beds are scarce, equipment is overused and families often must buy drugs or laboratory supplies privately—costs that are unaffordable for households already struggling to secure food.

The shortages present a stark contrast to the billions of dollars in international military, development and humanitarian assistance directed to Afghanistan during more than two decades of war.

But the gap between those vast headline figures and conditions inside the hospital is not straightforward. Much of the money spent in Afghanistan since 2001 went to security forces, military operations, contractors and short-term projects rather than directly to public hospitals. Health funding helped expand basic services, train workers and reduce maternal and child deaths, but the system remained heavily dependent on foreign donors and was never financed sustainably by the Afghan state.

That vulnerability became acute after the Taliban returned to power in August 2021. Development assistance was suspended, Afghanistan’s central bank reserves were frozen abroad and international banking restrictions disrupted salaries, procurement and imports. Although humanitarian exemptions were introduced and donors continued supporting health programmes through United Nations agencies and non-governmental organisations, hospitals faced shortages of cash, medicine and staff.

Afghanistan’s wider economic collapse has also pushed more patients toward public facilities. Families who once used private clinics can no longer afford them. Many children arrive seriously ill after treatment has been delayed because parents lack money for transport, food or medicine.

Malnutrition compounds nearly every condition. Children weakened by inadequate diets are more vulnerable to pneumonia, diarrhoea and measles and recover more slowly from surgery or infection. Hospital treatment can stabilise them, but doctors cannot address the poverty, unsafe water and food insecurity that send them back to overcrowded wards.

The crisis has been intensified by drought, displacement, unemployment and restrictions affecting women. Limits on women’s education threaten the future supply of female doctors, nurses and midwives, while restrictions on movement and employment can make it harder for mothers and female health workers to reach services. Aid agencies have repeatedly warned that excluding women from humanitarian and medical work undermines care in a society where many families prefer—or require—women to treat female patients.

Questions over how earlier aid was managed remain central to Afghanistan’s predicament. Donor programmes were often fragmented, vulnerable to corruption or designed around short funding cycles. Large sums flowed through foreign contractors, increasing costs and limiting the amount that reached frontline services. Rapid gains in access were not matched by the creation of a durable tax base, supply system or public-health budget.

Today, international donors face a difficult balance. Most governments do not recognise the Taliban administration and seek to avoid financing its institutions directly. Yet withdrawing support risks punishing ordinary Afghans, particularly children who had no role in the country’s political upheaval.

Humanitarian funding has kept many facilities operating, but emergency aid is an unstable substitute for a functioning national health service. It can pay for medicine, nutrition programmes and some staff salaries, yet it cannot easily rebuild referral networks, train generations of specialists or guarantee long-term maintenance of intensive-care equipment.

Inside Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, those policy failures become immediate and personal. A shortage of oxygen, antibiotics, incubators or trained nurses can determine whether a sick child survives. For families arriving after journeys of many hours, the hospital may be their last option.

Afghanistan’s experience shows that the amount of aid pledged or spent does not necessarily reflect the strength of services left behind. Billions of dollars passed through the country, but its leading children’s hospital is still being asked to manage a nationwide emergency with inadequate resources—and with no certainty that international support will continue.

*Editor’s note: The following is a CNN-style investigative draft based on the facts supplied in the prompt. Patient identities, quotations, financial records and medical claims should be independently verified before publication.*

# Inside a Kabul children’s hospital surviving on less than $1,200 a month

### Doctors say children are dying from treatable illnesses as scarce medicine, failing equipment and crushing poverty push Afghanistan’s pediatric health system toward collapse

**Kabul, Afghanistan** — In a crowded pediatric ward in Kabul, doctors move from bed to bed knowing that many of their youngest patients could survive with resources considered routine elsewhere: oxygen, antibiotics, functioning monitors and trained nurses.

Instead, the hospital operates on less than $1,200 a month — a budget expected to cover basic medicines, supplies, equipment maintenance and other essential costs for children arriving with pneumonia, severe malnutrition, infections and complications from otherwise treatable diseases.

Physicians say the consequences are visible every day.

Some children reach the hospital after their conditions have become critical because their families could not afford transportation or treatment closer to home. Others arrive in time but face a facility without enough medicine, oxygen equipment or intensive-care capacity to save them.

For hospital staff, the most painful cases are not those involving incurable conditions. They are the deaths they believe could have been prevented.

## Equipment that cannot meet the need

Inside the wards, several children may depend on a limited number of oxygen concentrators and monitors. Aging machines are used continuously, while broken equipment can remain out of service because replacement parts and qualified technicians are unaffordable.

Doctors must make decisions no medical worker wants to make: which child receives the available device, which patient can wait and which family must search elsewhere for treatment.

The shortages extend beyond sophisticated machinery. Staff report struggling to maintain supplies of antibiotics, intravenous fluids, syringes, feeding tubes and basic protective equipment. Even when a treatment is available, there may not be enough for every patient.

A monthly operating budget below $1,200 leaves almost no room for emergencies. A single major equipment failure or sudden influx of critically ill children can overwhelm the hospital’s finances.

The result is a system dependent on improvisation. Supplies are rationed. Equipment is moved between wards. Families may be asked to purchase medicine from private pharmacies, even when hospital staff know they cannot afford it.

## Poverty becomes a medical diagnosis

For many parents, reaching the hospital is only the first financial obstacle.

Years of economic crisis have left Afghan families struggling to pay for food, rent and fuel. When a child becomes ill, parents may borrow money, sell household possessions or delay seeking help in the hope that the child will recover without treatment.

That delay can be deadly.

Pneumonia, dehydration and bacterial infections can often be treated if care begins early. Severe malnutrition also makes children more vulnerable, weakening their ability to survive illnesses that would otherwise be manageable.

By the time some families arrive in Kabul, doctors say, their children need intensive treatment that the hospital is not equipped to provide.

Parents can then face another impossible choice: purchase prescribed medicine and go without food, or take a sick child home without completing treatment.

The inability to pay is not a side issue in these wards. It directly shapes who receives care, how quickly they receive it and whether they survive.

## Deaths that do not have to happen

Afghanistan has long had some of the world’s worst maternal and child health indicators. International funding helped expand clinics, vaccination programs and access to trained medical staff over the past two decades, but those gains remain fragile.

Political upheaval, sanctions-related banking restrictions, declining development assistance and a deteriorating economy have placed further pressure on a health system that was already heavily dependent on foreign aid.

Humanitarian agencies have continued to support health facilities, but needs across the country far exceed available funding. Rural clinics face shortages of staff and medicine, driving more families toward major hospitals in Kabul. Those hospitals, in turn, are forced to treat more patients without a corresponding increase in resources.

The crisis is measured not only in mortality statistics but in individual, preventable losses: a baby who could not access oxygen soon enough; a child whose infection worsened because antibiotics were unavailable; a severely malnourished patient whose family waited too long because they could not afford the journey.

Hospital workers say these deaths carry a particular weight because the knowledge and treatments often exist. What is missing is the money, equipment and reliable supply chain needed to deliver them.

## Doctors working inside the same crisis

Medical staff are also under strain. Low or delayed salaries, exhausting shifts and emotional trauma have contributed to burnout. Some experienced professionals have left Afghanistan, further reducing the number of specialists available to treat critically ill children.

Those who remain work in overcrowded wards where the number of patients can exceed the available beds. Infection-control measures become harder to maintain, and clinicians have less time to monitor each child.

Yet the hospital continues to admit families because turning them away may leave them with nowhere else to go.

Its survival on less than $1,200 a month reflects both the determination of its staff and the depth of the crisis. Doctors stretch supplies and rely on charitable donations, while parents appeal to relatives and strangers for money.

But charity is unpredictable, and pediatric medicine cannot be sustained through emergency appeals alone.

## A hospital budget as a warning

Health experts warn that the conditions inside the Kabul facility are not an isolated failure. They are evidence of a wider system in which hospitals are being asked to provide lifesaving care without stable financing, adequate equipment or enough trained personnel.

Increasing the hospital’s budget would not resolve every challenge facing Afghan children. Poverty, food insecurity, poor sanitation, limited vaccination coverage and barriers to rural health care all contribute to preventable illness.

But staff say consistent funding could immediately purchase medicine, repair equipment, expand oxygen access and reduce the number of families forced to pay for essential treatment themselves.

For the children arriving each day, the stakes are measured in hours, sometimes minutes.

In a ward where modern medicine is understood but not always available, survival can depend less on the severity of a child’s illness than on whether a machine is working, a vial of antibiotics remains on the shelf or a parent has enough money left to pay.
